title: Flame Tests

stepCard.title: Step card
steps: Dip a fresh splint in one salt. Hold it at the edge of the flame for 10 seconds.
Record the color and the brightness.
Test all six salts and NaNO3 (the control).
Take unknown bottles A and B. Test them.
If two knowns match, use the spectroscope.
Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

tutorial2: The spectroscope splits flame light into its colors.
Each line is one color the metal gives out.
Same crimson to the eye, different lines.
specGuide: Each black row is what a spectroscope shows for one metal. Each bright line is one color of light that metal gives out, placed at its wavelength; the strip on top shows which color sits where. Look first at where the lines fall, then compare with the other rows. Sr has a blue line near 461 nm; Li has none. That separates the two crimson metals. Wrong reading: a taller or thicker line does not tell you how bright the flame looked. The faint glow behind Sr and Cu is a wide band. The two K lines at the far right are at the edge of vision.
swatchGuide: Each box is the flame color you will see, with its name underneath. Look first at the two Na boxes: they match on purpose. Watch for Li and Sr: those two boxes are identical too, and that is the problem the lab ends on.
intro: Today you test salts in a flame and name two unknowns from the colors.
introSteps: Do the pre-lab: three pictures and one prediction. The lab door stays shut until you finish.
Huddle 1: Mr. D gives you the first code.
Suit up, go to the flame bench, and follow the step card.
Test six salts and NaNO3, then unknown bottles A and B.
Write your claim, evidence and reasoning. Huddle 2 comes after your data.
keyRows: Use what you are facing (locker, shelf, bench, door).
Step away from the bench, or close a window.
Point at anything to see its name.

cerUi.evidenceHint: Tick results from your own table that support the claim. Pick at least two.
cerUi.reasoningHint: Say why that evidence points to that metal, or why it cannot decide. Evidence says what happened; reasoning says why it matters.
